CweFindings.Name: Unchecked Input for Loop Condition
CweFindings.Description: The product does not properly check inputs that are used for loop conditions, potentially leading to a denial of service or other consequences because of excessive looping.
CweFindings.Explanation: HomeController.uploadPhotos checks only null/empty at lines 63-67 and iterates every multipart element at lines 69-90, with per-file database processing. The configured app.file-upload.max-files-per-upload=10 at application.properties:30 is never consumed or enforced; upload count controls iteration and result-list growth. The 50MB multipart byte cap (lines 24-25) bounds bytes but not the intended application file-count/work limit; many small parts can force excessive per-file work. Endpoint requires authentication; servlet-container multipart defaults may impose an additional implementation-dependent ceiling.

CweFindings.Name: Memory Allocation with Excessive Size Value
CweFindings.Description: The product allocates memory based on an untrusted, large size value, but it does not ensure that the size is within expected limits, allowing arbitrary amounts of memory to be allocated.
CweFindings.Explanation: HomeController.index at lines 38-42 loads the entire gallery through PhotoServiceImpl.getAllPhotos:54-56. PhotoRepository.findAllOrderByUploadedAtDesc at lines 23-29 selects every row including photo_data with no page/row/aggregate-byte bound, and Photo.photoData at lines 39-41 is an eager-by-default byte[] LOB. As uploaded data accumulates, a public GET / materializes unbounded database-backed photo bytes and entities into JVM memory despite each upload being individually size-limited. This is aggregate allocation driven by uploaded content and database cardinality, not an assertion that the already-limited file.getBytes call is itself unbounded.

CweFindings.Name: Insufficient Logging
CweFindings.Description: When a security-critical event occurs, the product either does not record the event or omits important details about the event when logging it.
CweFindings.Explanation: DetailController.deletePhoto logs successful destructive operations at lines 64-70 with only the photo ID, and PhotoServiceImpl.deletePhoto repeats an ID-only event at lines 191-204. Neither records the authenticated principal or request/source identity; no application MDC/audit interceptor supplying actor context was identified. Thus a security-critical deletion omits who performed the action even though SecurityConfig requires authentication. This finding concerns missing audit details in existing logs, not an unverified claim that Spring never logs authentication failures.

CweFindings.Name: Unrestricted Upload of File with Dangerous Type
CweFindings.Description: The product allows the upload or transfer of dangerous file types that are automatically processed within its environment.
CweFindings.Explanation: PhotoServiceImpl.uploadPhoto trusts the multipart Content-Type allowlist (lines 86-93); no ImageReader at lines 124-143 is not a rejection, and non-IO dimension-reading exceptions are ignored at lines 149-152. Arbitrary non-image bytes with an allowed image MIME type therefore reach database persistence at lines 154-166 and are publicly returned unchanged by PhotoFileController.servePhoto at lines 74-83. File contents are not required to match an allowed image format; no server-side code execution is asserted.

CweFindings.Name: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting')
CweFindings.Description: The product does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes user-controllable input before it is placed in output that is used as a web page that is served to other users.
CweFindings.Explanation: upload.js createPhotoCard interpolates the original uploaded filename into HTML text and attributes at lines 181-190, then displayNewPhotos parses that string using insertAdjacentHTML at lines 155-157. HomeController.uploadPhotos returns the original filename at lines 75-79. A crafted filename containing HTML or attribute delimiters becomes executable markup in the uploading browser; server-rendered Thymeleaf pages escape this field, so cross-user persisted execution is not asserted. The same file also builds upload error HTML from filenames at lines 215-218.

CweFindings.Name: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command ('SQL Injection')
CweFindings.Description: The product constructs all or part of an SQL command using externally-influenced input from an upstream component, but it does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes special elements that could modify the intended SQL command when it is sent to a downstream component. Without sufficient removal or quoting of SQL syntax in user-controllable inputs, the generated SQL query can cause those inputs to be interpreted as SQL instead of ordinary user data.
CweFindings.Explanation: Database initialization uses configuration-derived APP_USER, uppercases but does not quote-escape it (01-create-user.sh:13-17), then embeds it in a SQL string literal at line 25 and dynamic DDL at lines 28 and 33-43. APP_USER_PASSWORD is likewise interpolated into CREATE USER at line 28. create-user.sh repeats this construction at lines 19 and 27-35. SQL metacharacters in configuration can alter the SQL interpreted by sqlplus under SYSTEM. This is a deployment/configuration trust-boundary issue, not an HTTP SQL injection; application repository queries use bind parameters.
